newsitem.title: UK: Russian political worry may tarnish Bunds, mark.
newsitem.headline: Russian political worry may tarnish Bunds, mark.

text.p: German bonds and the mark might lose some of their shine amid concern about Russian President Boris Yeltin's health but the impact will be only slight, at least for now, analysts said on Thursday.
German assets used to be hyper-sensitive to Russian risk because of bank loans, trade flows and geographical proximity.
But the end of the Cold War, coupled with progressive economic liberation in Russia, changed the situation considerably, the analysts said.
For now, the market impact of Yeltsin's illness would be marginal but a more significant shift could come if he died, leaving Russia leaderless and unstable, they added.
Yeltsin, who only returned to the Kremlin on December 23 after recovering from heart surgery in November, was taken into hospital again on Wednesday suffering from pneumonia.
Although his condition is described as "quite satisfactory", concern about the 65-year-old's health is already seeping into foreign exchange markets.

"The key question is the impact on the German mark, which has traditionally always been highly exposed to eastern Europe," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"But I'm a sceptic when it comes to the influence of Russia on the markets now. Russian/Western relationships have become enormously multilateral.

"But there will still always be a small impact on the deutschemark. Clearly, when things start to go badly in Russia, the dollar recommends itself because people begin to worry about whether a bi-polar world will emerge again," he said.
The dollar is expected to remain firm as news about Yeltsin's latest illness filters through, providing an impetus for switching out of core European bond markets into U.S. T-bonds, analysts said.
"Yeltsin's illness provides another reason to buy Treasuries," said Adrian Owens at Julius Baer Investments.
"With the 10-year yield spread to Bunds at 74 basis points, the U.S. market is looking quite attractive."

If Yeltsin died, analysts predict a sharp knee-jerk reaction, with the dollar likely to jolt higher against the mark, pulling Treasuries into outperformance and tightening the T-bond/German Bund 10-year yield gap.
Beyond the early days, it would be a question of watching and waiting.

Political commentators say stability may well be maintained, with Anatoly Chubais, the chief of the Kremlin administration, and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin stepping in to hold the fort, as they did when Yeltsin was out of action in November.
But Alexander Lebed, sacked by the Kremlin in October after he warned of potential mutiny within the army, has said that Yeltsin's illness left a political vacuum and called for him to resign.
"The assumption will be that Chernomyrdin will take over in the near term. But if things start to get really messy further down the road, markets will see more of an impact," said Owens.
The main fear would be the risk to the process of economic reform presented by any change in leadership, said Nick Stamenkovic, European economist at DKB International in London.
If progress was hampered, investment in Russia would begin to dry up, prompting negative market sentiment towards Bunds and the mark, he said.
But Stamenkovic said significant market gyrations were unlikely to arise from the Russian political situation.
"Traditionally when you have problems in Russia it has a damaging impact on the Bund market," he said. "But each time we have had problems, the impact has been less and less.
"This could have an immediate negative effect on Germany but I don't think it will be sustained."
